---
title: "Independent sampling"
---

The [preceding page](populations-and-samples.qmd) distinguished the target population from the realized sample. We now need a probability model that connects repeated samples to a population parameter. Suppose we sample four clauses and record whether each has an overt subject.

$$
X_i=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if clause }i\text{ has an overt subject},\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

To connect these observations to one population probability, we need a sampling model. A common starting point treats the observations as [**independent and identically distributed (IID)**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). We will treat the two adjectives separately because they license different later steps.

## Stating the identical distribution claim

Assume every clause has the same Bernoulli distribution:

$$
X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi)
$$

for every $i$. This says

$$
\mathbb{P}(X_i=1)=\pi
$$

for each observation. The overt subject probability does not change across clause positions under the model.

This is the *identically distributed* part of the IID assumption. It is a claim about the modeled PMF, not a claim that all observed clauses have the same realized value.

## Adding independence conditional on the parameter

Now assume that once $\pi$ is fixed, the complete collection of clause outcomes is mutually independent. This is the [independence condition introduced in the foundations module](../foundations/independence.qmd), applied conditionally on a shared parameter:

$$
 p(x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid\pi)
=\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i\mid\pi).
$$

Mutual independence is stronger than checking each pair separately. It is the assumption that justifies the product for the complete sample.

Together, the assumptions are written

$$
X_1,\ldots,X_n
\mathrel{\overset{\mathrm{IID}}{\sim}}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi).
$$

The parameter $\pi$ is shared; the realized outcomes may differ.

## Factoring the probability of a sample

Suppose the observed sequence is

$$
(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(1,0,1,1).
$$

The [probability chain rule](../foundations/probability-factorization.qmd) first gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\mid\pi)
={}&p(x_1\mid\pi)\\
&\times p(x_2\mid x_1,\pi)\\
&\times p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2,\pi)\\
&\times p(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3,\pi).
\end{aligned}
$$

Conditional independence removes the earlier observations from each later factor:

$$
p(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\mid\pi)
=\prod_{i=1}^{4}p(x_i\mid\pi).
$$

For the observed sequence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(1,0,1,1\mid\pi)
&=\pi(1-\pi)\pi\pi\\
&=\pi^3(1-\pi).
\end{aligned}
$$

The product is a consequence of the independence assumption. It is not an algebraic convenience that can be used regardless of sampling structure.

## Evaluating one candidate probability

If $\pi=.60$, then

$$
p(1,0,1,1\mid.60)
=(.60)^3(.40)
=.0864.
$$

This is the probability of that exact ordered sequence. The probability of any sequence containing three overt subjects among four clauses is larger because there are four placements for the single zero.

```{r}
#| eval: false
pi_overt <- .60
sequence_probability <- pi_overt^3 * (1 - pi_overt)
three_of_four_probability <- choose(4, 3) * sequence_probability

c(sequence_probability, three_of_four_probability)
```

The distinction between one sequence and an unordered count will matter when likelihoods are written from different data representations.

## Asking whether linguistic rows are plausible IID units

Clauses from one speaker may share that speaker's subject realization tendency. Clauses in one document may share genre, topic, or discourse structure. These repetitions can violate independence.

The identical distribution claim may also fail. Questions, subordinate clauses, and imperatives can have different overt subject probabilities even when sampled independently.

Ten clauses from one speaker are ten clause observations. They are not equivalent to ten independently sampled speakers when the population claim concerns speaker variation.

## Distinct rows need not be independent

A unique key establishes that two rows are different observations. It does not make the observations independent or remove their shared speaker, item, or document.

Specify the proposed independent unit and list the identifiers repeated across rows. Later models represent those repeated sources directly.

## Check your understanding

1. Under the IID Bernoulli model, write the probability of the sequence $(0,1,0)$.
2. Explain the difference between identically distributed observations and identical observed values.
3. Which assumption justifies replacing conditional factors with $p(x_i\mid\pi)$?
4. Give one corpus structure that could violate independence and one that could violate the shared probability claim.
